passage: I'm Isha, and I was sitting two rows behind when a lab assistant told Manoj, in front of everyone, that people from his part of the country "never finish on time." Manoj went still. Dhruv shot to his feet. "I'm going straight to the head of department. Right now. I'll sort this out for you." I saw Manoj tug his sleeve, and I saw a flicker cross Manoj's face that I can't name. Dhruv stopped. He sat down, took a breath and asked, "What do you want here? Tell me and I'll back you." Manoj said quietly that he wanted to speak to the coordinator himself. On Friday they went together. Manoj talked and Dhruv stood a step behind him, saying nothing at all until Manoj looked over.

qa.q: What did the lab assistant say about people from Manoj's part of the country?
qa.a: The lab assistant said they "never finish on time."

qa.q: Why did Dhruv stop and sit down after Manoj tugged his sleeve?
qa.a: Dhruv seemed to realise he was speaking over Manoj and wanted to ask what Manoj wanted, though Isha says the reason cannot be known for sure.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that supported Manoj's voice?
qa.a: He asked what Manoj wanted, then stood a step behind while Manoj spoke to the coordinator himself.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt if Dhruv had gone straight to the head of department?
qa.a: Manoj might have felt helpless or sidelined, as though the situation had become Dhruv's story instead of his own.

grounding: A friend faces bias and the protagonist first wants to shield him, then asks what he wants and supports his own voice.

passage:
In Ratlam the district cricket trials were on Sunday, and the coach had told Wasim, in front of everyone, that "your kind" never lasted in the team. Madhav heard about it at the tea stall and saw red. He was already planning the speech he would give the coach, the post he would write, the uncles he would call.

At home his sister Damini was folding clothes. "Did you ask Wasim what he wants?"

"He'll want me to fight for him."

"Will he? Or will he feel like a child who needs rescuing?"

Madhav went to Wasim's house that evening. "What do you want to do? I'm with you either way."

Wasim was quiet a long time. "I want to play on Sunday. If he says it again, I'll complain to the association myself. Just stand next to me."

On Sunday Madhav stood by the boundary rope. Wasim scored forty-two.

qa.q: How many runs did Wasim score on Sunday?
What was Madhav feeling when he heard about the coach's comment?
qa.a: Madhav felt furious and fiercely protective, already planning speeches and calls on Wasim's behalf.

qa.q: How did Damini's question change Madhav's approach?
qa.a: Damini made Madhav ask Wasim what he wanted, so Madhav supported Wasim's own plan instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt if Madhav had fought the coach without asking?
qa.a: Wasim might have felt helpless and spoken over, as if his own story had been taken from him.

grounding: The story shows a young man wanting to shield a friend from bias who learns to ask what his friend wants and support his voice.

passage:
At the café in Stockholm where they both worked weekends, the new manager kept giving Jamal the back room and the dish pit, never the counter. On Tuesday he said to Jamal, loud enough to hear, "Customers prefer a more Swedish face at the front."

Anders felt heat rush up his neck. Before Jamal could answer, Anders stepped in. "That's discrimination. You can't say that. I'm reporting you."

On the walk home Jamal was silent. Finally he said, "You made it about you, man. I didn't get to say anything."

Anders stopped on the bridge. His first instinct was to defend himself. Instead he asked, "You're right. What do you want to do?"

"I want to write the complaint. In my words. You can sign as a witness."

They wrote it together that night at Jamal's kitchen table, Jamal typing, Anders reading over his shoulder only when asked.

qa.q: What did the manager say customers preferred?
qa.a: He said customers prefer a more Swedish face at the front.

qa.q: How did Anders feel when the manager spoke, and what did he do?
qa.a: Anders felt angry and protective, and stepped in to confront the manager before Jamal could answer.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Anders spoke over Jamal and made it his own fight; asking Jamal what he wanted and acting as a witness fixed it.

qa.q: How did Jamal experience Anders stepping in?
qa.a: Jamal felt sidelined, as if the moment had been taken from him, even though Anders meant well.

grounding: The story shows a young man protective of a friend facing bias who learns to support his friend's voice rather than speak over him.
